title: What's new with the Neon backend - Neon
text:
# What's new with the Neon backend

A roundup of what we've shipped lately across Lakebase Postgres, Managed Better Auth, Functions, Object Storage, AI Gateway, and Realtime

Carlota Soto– Product Team

Nov 10, 2026

Neon now includes a complete set of backend primitives - the database (Lakebase Postgres), Managed Better Auth, Functions, Object Storage, AI Gateway, and we just launched Realtime in beta. We ship updates to all of them every week, which we list in our changelog - this post rounds up a few of the recent ones worth knowing about.

## What's new with Lakebase Postgres

#### Lakebase Postgres

Lakebase Postgres is the Neon database: serverless Postgres that scales and branches with your app, built on object storage and the WAL. It takes you from your first users to the Fortune 500, with coding agents as a first-class interface.

### More storage on the Free plan

The Neon Free Plan now includes 1 GB of Postgres storage per project, up from 0.5 GB.

...

### Operational updates

- Automatic updates for computes up to 16 CU - Every compute up to 16 CU, including all autoscaling computes, now gets compute updates automatically. An update restarts the compute in a few seconds, and Neon prewarms the cache so queries don't run cold afterward. On paid plans, updates run in the window you choose.
- More read replicas for paid plans - they now support up to 6 read replicas per branch
- Recover deleted projects from the console - A deleted project can be recovered for 7 days, now from the Console as well as the CLI and API
- Least-privilege roles for agents -`neon roles create --access read_only` (or `read_write`) creates a scoped role instead of an admin. The same option is on the Neon MCP Server, and the MCP Server can now run every SQL tool as a Postgres role you choose, so the role's grants decide what an agent can read and change.

## Just shipped in Neon Functions

#### Neon Functions

Neon Functions are long-running serverless functions right next to your database. You can use them in the Free plan, with 10 active Capacity-Hours, 400 waiting Capacity-Hours, and 1 million invocations per project each month.

...

### Use AI Gateway from the Free Plan

Every Neon user can now buy AI Gateway credits, starting at $5, including on the Free plan. Once you add credits, you can call every model in the catalog at the same per-token price you'd pay using the labs' own APIs.

title: Neon Pricing 2026: Plans, Free Tier Limits, and Costs
text:
Summary

Choose Neon's entry paid plan for small production teams, Free for hobbies, and higher tiers for branches or compliance requirements.

- Free plan hard-caps compute and storage, so outgrown projects stall instead of scaling.
- Compute is roughly 64 per cent of the monthly bill for production databases.
- Each extra branch beyond your plan's included allowance incurs a cost of $1.50 per branch-month.

...

Neon pricing is the set of plan tiers, from Free through paid usage-based plans, that determine how many compute hours and how much storage a Neon Postgres project includes each month and what it costs when you exceed them.

...

- The right plan is the one whose included allowance covers your real compute hours and data size
- For most small teams running production, that's the entry paid plan rather than Free
- Free is built for experiments, and the first month of real traffic usually shows why
- The meter is compute-hours: any process that wakes the database, including scheduled jobs or automated flows, spends from the same allowance as your users do

The table below shows four common situations, the plan that fits each, what it costs, and the catch that pushes you up a tier. It's accurate as of November 2026.

Neon revises its allowances and rates, so confirm them on its pricing page before you commit.

| Reader situation | Plan | Monthly cost | Catch that pushes up a tier |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Small production team | Entry paid plan | No minimum monthly fee, usage-based billing | Steady compute hours or growing storage that drive up usage charges |
| Bursty app with preview branches | Entry paid plan, then a higher tier | Base fee plus metered usage, rising with branch count | Each active branch consumes compute and storage, so the bill tracks how many you leave running |
| Compliance-bound team | A higher paid tier | No minimum monthly fee, usage-based billing | Security and admin features sit above the entry plan |

For a solo or hobby project, stay on Free. It costs nothing, and a side project that sleeps most of the day will rarely touch the compute allowance.

...

## Neon plans side by side

Free, Launch and Scale differ on nine dimensions, set out in the table below. The table shows how the plans are structured.

### How Neon bills: compute-hours, storage and CUs

You are billed on the compute unit (CU), a slice of CPU and memory. Neon multiplies the CUs your database uses by the hours it's awake, which gives CU-hours. Neon meters storage separately, and branches add to it.

Once a database scales to zero when idle, it stops accruing CU-hours, so an always-on production database costs far more than a dev database with the same schema.

Before usage charges begin, each plan includes an allowance of CU-hours and storage.

> Once a database scales to zero when idle, it stops accruing CU-hours, so an always-on production database costs far more than a dev database with the same schema.

### Neon pricing table with verified values

I assembled the table on 2 November 2026 from Neon's pricing page and docs. Where I couldn't confirm a value, the cell says so.

| | Free | Launch | Scale |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Base price | No monthly fee | No minimum monthly fee, pay for what you use | No minimum monthly fee, pay for what you use |
| CU-hours | Fixed included allowance, size unverified | Usage-based, allowance unverified | Usage-based, allowance unverified |
| Storage | Capped, size unverified | Unverified | Unverified |
| Projects | Limited, count unverified | Unverified | Unverified |
| Branches | Limited, count unverified | Unverified | Unverified |
| Autoscaling max | Lowest of the three, size unverified | Unverified | Highest of the three, size unverified |
| Restore window | Shortest of the three, length unverified | Unverified | Longest of the three, length unverified |
| Support | Community | Unverified | Unverified |
| Compliance | Not the tier for regulated workloads | Unverified | Unverified |

Read the table in two passes. First compare the rows that scale with load: CU-hours, storage and branches. Those decide your bill. Then compare restore window and compliance, which decide whether a plan is safe for production at all.

Since Databricks acquired Neon, pricing has moved. Check any older comparison or blog post against the live page.

...

### Do discounts exist?

To confirm any startup or annual-billing discount, the pricing page is the only place, and the body's math assumes list price.

If a startup program or annual option exists when you read this, it lowers the cost of the entry paid plan. It doesn't change which plan matches your compute hours and storage.

title: Neon vs Supabase: Which is cheaper for a small app? Compare $0 free tiers, $0.106 CU-hours, and $25 Pro plans | Costbrake
text:
## Paid plan mechanics: Hourly pay-as-you-go vs $25 base fees

Neon's paid tiers (Launch and Scale) use pure pay-as-you-go billing with hourly metering and no monthly minimums. If your total invoice is under $0.50 at the end of the month, Neon does not even collect it. Launch compute costs $0.106 per CU-hour, while storage costs $0.35 per GB-month measured hourly. Scale-to-zero is enabled by default with a 5-minute inactivity window, but you can turn it off if you need a database that never sleeps.

Supabase Pro takes the opposite approach by charging a predictable $25 monthly subscription up front. That base fee covers your first project, and extra projects cost from $10 per month. The plan gives you $10 per month in compute credits, which exactly covers a Micro instance (1 GB RAM, shared CPU at $0.01344 per hour). It also bundles 8 GB of gp3 disk, 250 GB of public egress, 250 GB of cached egress, 100 GB of file storage, and 100,000 monthly active users.

If you run multiple small databases for side projects, Neon lets you create up to 100 projects on Launch without paying a fixed base fee for each one. On Supabase, five active projects on Pro will cost you at least $65 a month ($25 base plus four extra projects at $10 each) before factoring in any extra resources.

...

| Feature or Resource | Neon Launch | Supabase Pro |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Starting price | $0/mo (pay-as-you-go) | $25/mo (billed up front) |
| Additional projects | Included (up to 100) | From $10/mo each |
| Smallest paid compute | 0.25 CU (1 GB RAM): $0.0265/hr | Micro (1 GB RAM): $0.01344/hr |
| Compute credit included | None | $10/mo (covers 1 Micro instance) |
| Scale-to-zero | Yes (5 min default, can disable) | No (runs 24/7 unless paused) |
| Database storage price | $0.35/GB-month | 8 GB included, then $0.125/GB |
| Egress allowance | 500 GB/project included, then $0.10/GB | 250 GB included, then $0.09/GB |
| Point-in-time recovery | $0.20/GB-month (root history) | $100/mo per 7 days retention |
| Database branching | 10 included, then $1.50/mo | $0.01344/branch/hr (~$10/mo) |
| Spend cap | API consumption limits & email alerts | Spend cap toggle (covers 12 items) |

Neon beats Supabase's free project allowance and database size: 100 projects and 1 GB per project, with a 20 GB account total, versus 2 active projects and a 500 MB database.

It also handles inactivity differently. Supabase Free pauses after 1 week; Neon scales compute to zero after 5 minutes and restarts on the next query, typically within a few hundred milliseconds. Suspended compute costs $0.

Launch charges $0.106 per CU-hour and $0.35 per GB-month of database storage. It includes 500 GB public network transfer per project, then charges $0.10/GB.

But is the bill capped? Spending notifications don't stop usage. Set autoscaling limits and per-project consumption limits through the Neon API; consumption limits suspend compute at the quota.

...

Neon Launch has no monthly minimum or per-project fee, with typical small-database spend around $15 per month versus Supabase Pro starting at $25. That typical spend isn't a quote for your workload.

Packaging November 6, 2026

# Neon opens its AI Gateway to Free plan accounts

Neon pricing

AI Gateway: paid plans only, not included in the Free plan AI Gateway: every plan, including Free, with prepaid credits and a card on file

Until this month a developer who wanted Neon’s single API for OpenAI, Google and other models had to move off the Free plan first, which on Neon means starting to pay for every CU-hour from zero. Now the model calls can be bought on their own: a Free organization adds a card, buys credits, and its database, storage and egress allowances stay as they were.

The pricing is unchanged: requests are charged at each model provider’s list price with no markup, drawn from prepaid credits, and the same $2 minimum balance and default $20 a day spend cap apply. One thing Free accounts do not get yet is automatic top-up, so a Free app that runs out of credits stops getting model responses until someone buys more.

What it means for buyers. If you prototype AI features on Neon’s Free plan, you no longer need a paid plan to call models through the gateway. Budget for manual top-ups, and treat a $5 purchase as the smallest unit of spend.

Technical evidence

Before kind (A): the 2026-10-31 cloud-vm capture of the AI Gateway prepaid-credits docs (listed as US-verified by the baseline tool) reads “The AI Gateway is available on paid Neon plans only. It is not included in the Free plan.”, and the same day’s pricing-page capture reads “AI Gateway is available on Launch and Scale.” The 2026-11-09 captures of both pages state availability on every plan, including Free. The date comes from the vendor’s changelog entry of 2026-11-06, “All accounts can purchase AI Gateway credits”.

title: Supabase vs Neon vs PlanetScale: Free-Tier Traps + Real Migration Cost (2026) | beyondimy
text:
Two years ago the playbook was "host everything on a free PlanetScale Hobby plan." Then PlanetScale killed that plan in April 2024, and Neon and Supabase became the default free starts for Postgres, while Turso carved out a niche with serverless SQLite. Fast-forward to November 2026 and the map changed again — Neon is now part of Databricks, and Supabase announced it was acquiring Turso in October 2026 [ref: Turso acquisition blog post, 2026-10-02].

...

- Supabase Free (500 MB DB, 5 GB egress) pauses your project after 1 week of inactivity — a trap for low-traffic apps, not busy ones. Exceeding 500 MB sends the DB read-only at 95% disk. No automatic backups: you own your `supabase db dump`.
- Neon Free (1 GB storage, 100 CU-hours per project, 5 GB egress) never pauses for inactivity — scale-to-zero handles that — but exhausted CU-hours suspend compute and full storage blocks writes until the next billing cycle or an upgrade. Data is never deleted.
- PlanetScale has no free tier. The Hobby plan was retired April 8, 2024 and never replaced; entry pricing starts around $5/month for dev workloads, Metal from ~$50/month.
- Turso Free (5 GB storage, 500M rows read, 10M rows written, 100 DBs) is generous but SQLite-shaped — exceeding limits means upgrading, since overage billing on Free doesn't exist. And since Oct 2026 Turso is joining Supabase.
- Postgres→Postgres migration is near-free: one `pg_dump`/`pg_restore` pass, minutes of downtime. MySQL→Postgres and SQLite→Postgres are the expensive ones — schema rewrites, boolean/enum conversions, driver changes.
- Realistic "graduated" spend for a solo dev: $15–25/month (Neon Launch small workload or Supabase Pro with spend caps), not $5.

## Free-Tier Facts Table (Nov 2026)

| | Supabase Free | Neon Free | Turso Free | PlanetScale |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Price | $0 | $0 | $0 | No free tier |
| DB storage | 500 MB DB size per project | 1 GB per project, 20 GB org total | 5 GB total | — |
| Compute quota | Shared CPU · 500 MB RAM instance | 100 CU-hours/project/mo, autoscale up to 2 CU | N/A (rows-based) | — |
| Egress / reads | 5 GB egress + 5 GB cached egress | 5 GB egress per project | 500M rows read, 10M rows written | — |
| Other caps | 2 active projects, 50k MAU, 1 GB file storage, 500k function invocations | 10 branches, 6h history, 1 snapshot, 60k auth MAU | 1-day PITR, community support | Entry ~$5/mo, Metal ~$50+/mo |
| Projects allowed | 2 active (pause/unpause trick for more) | 100 projects | 100 databases | — |
| Backups | None automatic — docs tell you to run `supabase db dump` yourself | 1 manual snapshot + 6h history (no scheduled backups) | 1-day PITR window | Paid plans only |
| The signature trap | Pause after 7 days of low activity | Compute suspension on CU-hour exhaustion | Rows-read/written caps | Free tier doesn't exist |

...

### Neon: the CU-hour meter and the write-block wall

Neon's free tier is the most generous and the most instrumented. It doesn't pause anything for inactivity — compute scales to zero after 5 minutes idle and cold-starts in "a few hundred milliseconds" (their words). A quiet Neon project on the Free plan stays alive forever, costing only the seconds it's awake.

But there's a monthly meter: 100 CU-hours per project. Running the floor-size 0.25 CU compute 24/7 burns ~180 CU-hours, so Free barely covers "always on" for one small project, and autoscaling can cap at 2 CU. When CU-hours run dry, or the 5 GB egress is exhausted, Neon suspends compute entirely until the next billing period or an upgrade — stated explicitly in Neon's pricing FAQ. Connection attempts fail rather than hang; data is intact.

Bigger than the CU-hour wall is the storage one: exceeding 1 GB per project (or 20 GB across the org) blocks writes — you can still read, query, and dump. Neon's guidance is a straight upgrade to Launch to lift it; they also offer credits to developers and startups, up to $100k via their Startup Program if you qualify. The escape hatch is clean regardless: Neon is vanilla Postgres, so `pg_dump` walks you out the door in under an hour for a small DB. The lock-in is pricing-tier shape, not data-format shape.

...

- Quiet side project that must stay reachable → Neon. No inactivity pause; scale-to-zero means silence costs nothing. Watch the 1 GB/project storage cap.
- Active hobby app using Auth + Storage + Postgres together → Supabase. Schedule a cron ping if traffic is thin, run scheduled `supabase db dump` for backups; graduation is one clean Pro ($25) block.
- Many isolated little DBs (per-tenant, per-experiment) → Neon Free (100 projects, separate quota each) or Turso Free (100 databases). Neon keeps the Postgres escape hatch; Turso locks you into SQLite-shape code.
- High-read, low-write, many small instances → Turso — 500M rows read/month for $0 is hard to beat — accepting its Oct 2026 Supabase orbit.
- Mission-critical or revenue-bearing → start paid from day one: PlanetScale (~$5/mo entry), Neon Launch, or Supabase Pro. Postgres→Postgres migration later costs an afternoon; MySQL→Postgres or SQLite→Postgres costs a day-plus of rewrite pain. Price that bill into your engine choice.

title: Save tokens with Neon Function templates - Neon
text:
# Save tokens with Neon Function templates

Introducing the Neon Function Registry. Add a template to your project with one command so your agent starts from working code.

Dominik Koch– DX Engineer

Nov 05, 2026

A few weeks ago we launched Neon Functions, Node.js functions that run in your Neon project in the same region as your Postgres database, with enough runtime for agents that stream for minutes or WebSockets that stay open.

Today we're introducing the Neon Function Registry, a collection of ready-made functions you add to a project with one command.

Agents can already bootstrap a function on their own, but before they write any code they read the docs, look up best practices, figure out `neon.ts` and pick package versions. All of that costs tokens and time.

With the registry, your agent starts from a working template and spends its time on something more useful like building your app.
